extracted.intended_audience: acquisitions librarians, bibliometricians, economists, journal editors, and researchers who evaluate journals
extracted.subtask_description: Selecting and evaluating a 'core' set of economics journals using Social Sciences Citation Index data; compares metrics such as citation frequency, impact factors, self-citation, and half-lives and discusses interpretation and caveats. Intended as a bibliometric guide for library acquisition and journal-ranking decisions in economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: How often a journal is cited; the main criterion for selecting the 'core' journals ("The main criterion for selecting journals for the core is their citation frequency—how often they are cited").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as primary selection filter but subject to caveats: journals with high citation counts may be eliminated if they have low impact or if high frequency is due to journal self-citation. Citation frequency in 1986 (from core journals) was used to form the core list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact factor (two-year)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact factor defined as 'the number of 1986 citations to 1984 and 1985 articles from a particular journal divided by the number of articles published in that journal in 1984 and 1985.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact factors can be computed using different base periods; the essay compares several base periods (1984–85, 1983–84, etc.) and notes relative rankings are robust to base-period choice. Impact is a measure of short-term citation intensity but must be interpreted in context of field citation timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal self-citation rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of citations to a journal that are citations from the same journal (self-citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High self-citation can inflate apparent citation frequency and impact; journals whose high citation frequency is largely due to self-citation were excluded from the core. The tables report self-citation percentages and the percent of core-journal citations that are self-citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent of total citations that are core-journal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of a journal's citations that come from the defined core journals (metric A/B in tables: citations from core journals divided by citations from all journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates how much a journal's influence is concentrated within the core set; used to understand inter-core connectivity and relative dependence on core vs non-core sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent of total citations that are self-citations (C/A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The percent of a journal's citations (to core journals) that are self-citations (table column E or C/A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported to show how much of a journal's apparent citation impact is internal; high values flag potential bias in raw citation counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cited half-life
rubrics_metrics.description: The median age of the articles from a journal that were being cited by other journals in 1986 ("the 1986 cited half-life of a journal is the median age of the articles from the journal that were being cited by other journals in 1986").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as evidence for article durability, accumulation of a large citable stock (long-lived journals), or possible decline in recent quality (older articles cited more than new ones). Long cited half-life may reflect theoretical focus or long existence; short half-life may indicate rapid obsolescence or fast-moving topical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing half-life
rubrics_metrics.description: The median age of the articles being cited by articles in the journal in 1986 (i.e., how far back the journal's authors cite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted in two ways: a low citing half-life can indicate authors are closer to the cutting edge (cite recent work); a high citing half-life may indicate more thorough scholarship or reliance on older, foundational literature. Editors may use this to characterize journal orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary language(s) in which a journal publishes (noted that core journals publish a majority of articles in English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language affects inclusion and interpretation: predominance of English implies geographic/language bias (e.g., U.S. as center of economic research). Journals publishing significant non-English content may be underrepresented in the core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal age / years of origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The founding year or longevity of a journal (tables list years of origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older journals accumulate a large 'stock' of citable articles which can lengthen cited half-life and influence metrics; founding date helps interpret long half-lives vs recent specialized journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization versus generality (field journals vs general journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal is a field/ specialized journal or a general/theoretical journal (the essay notes newer core journals tend to be field journals, and theoretical/general journals often rate higher in some rankings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization trends affect citation patterns—field journals may concentrate citations within subcommunities; theoretical/general journals may have broader influence and durability. Rankings and interpretation should consider journal scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate and turnaround time (author preferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics valued by authors (prestige, high acceptance rates, quick turnaround) used in authors' submission-order models (from Oster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oster's optimal submission ordering weights prestige, acceptance rate, and turnaround; the essay warns that if many authors act on such preferences the situation can be self-defeating (journals' acceptance rates and turnaround would change). These characteristics affect perceived desirability but are dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional affiliation of authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the institutional affiliations of article authors as a basis for ranking journals (a criterion used in previous studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional affiliation was one of several past ranking methods; correlations with citation-based measures vary. It can bias rankings toward journals favored by elite institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer evaluation / peer familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rankings based on peer judgments (surveys) about journal quality and familiarity among scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer evaluation correlates reasonably well with citation measures (noted high correlation in McDonough's work); it captures perceived quality but can reflect subjective or disciplinary biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance on graduate course reading lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting how often journal articles appear on graduate course reading lists as a quality/ranking indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects educational influence; used in prior ranking studies. May correlate differently with research impact compared to citation counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of subscribers / subscription-based ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ranking journals by number of subscribers (circulation) as an indicator of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subscription counts can mislead (e.g., Bell Journal ranked high because it was distributed free), so raw subscription numbers must be interpreted cautiously; distribution model affects this metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of citation sources (inclusion/exclusion of non-economics journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether citations from outside the economics field (non-economics journals) are included when counting citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including external-field citations can notably alter rankings (e.g., elevating interdisciplinary journals); excluding them may better reflect intra-field influence. Choice of citation universe affects results and should match the ranking purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted citation schemes / iterative weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Using weighted citation methods (e.g., iterative schemes) to adjust citation counts by the importance of citing journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighted schemes can correct biases and shift rankings (noted that field/historical journals moved up in one weighted ranking). Such methods are more complex but can provide a nuanced view of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination for low impact or high self-citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying filters to remove journals from the core if they have low impact or if high citation frequency is due to journal self-citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a quality-control step after raw citation counting to avoid including journals with artificially inflated citation counts or low influence despite frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing to peak influence (immediate impact vs staying power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that in economics articles often take several years (three to five) to reach peak influence; immediate citation impact may differ from long-term importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose base periods for impact calculations with awareness that economics citations often peak later; consider multi-period comparisons to assess both short-term and long-term influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total source items (number of source items)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total number of source items (articles) in a journal (listed in tables as '1986 source items').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in conjunction with citation counts to compute impact factor (denominator); larger or smaller output affects per-article measures and interpretation of raw citation totals.
